title: ReLU
body:
$$
\begin{matrix}
\text{ReLU} = \max\{0,z\} \\
\frac{d\text{ReLU}}{dz} = \begin{cases}
0 , \quad z<0 \\
1,\quad z>0
\end{cases}
\end{matrix}
$$
[[Leaky ReLU]]

---

Rectified Linear Unit, and **the default [[Activation Function]] for
[[Hidden Layer|hidden layers]]**. Two straight lines meeting at the origin, which is the least
interesting non-linear function imaginable, and that is the point: the single kink is enough to
satisfy [[Non-Linear]] and nothing else is paid for.

The derivative above is the whole reason it won. It is **exactly $1$** wherever the unit is active,
so the backward signal passes through untouched no matter how deep the stack goes. Compare
[[Sigmoid]], whose derivative peaks at $0.25$ and shrinks the gradient by at least $4^{-n}$ through
$n$ layers. That is the vanishing gradient problem, and ReLU simply does not have it. See
[[Chain Rule]] in [[CALCULUS 1]].

Three smaller advantages, all following from the formula:

- **Cheap.** A comparison and a select. No $e^{-z}$ anywhere, which matters when it runs on every
  unit of every layer of every example.
- **Sparse.** Roughly half the units output exactly zero on a given input, so each example
  activates a subset of the network rather than all of it.
- **Unbounded above.** It does not saturate for large positive $z$, so a strongly activated unit
  keeps learning.

## Dead units, the failure mode

The derivative is $0$ for $z < 0$, so a unit pushed into the negative region receives **no
gradient at all** and cannot be pushed back. It is not slow, it is stuck: that unit outputs zero
for every input, forever, and its [[Weights]] never change again. A large learning rate can kill a
sizeable fraction of a layer this way in one step. [[Leaky ReLU]] exists precisely to keep that
gradient non-zero.

Note that $z = 0$ has no derivative, since the left and right limits disagree. Implementations pick
$0$ (or $1$) and move on. It never matters in practice, because hitting exactly zero has
probability zero in floating point.
